newsitem.title: TAIWAN: China trade delegation to visit Taiwan - reports.
newsitem.headline: China trade delegation to visit Taiwan - reports.

text.p: Business leaders from China will visit rival Taiwan next week to promote economic and trade ties despite a frosty political impasse across the Taiwan strait, local newspapers said on Thursday.

Guo Dongpo, chairman of the China Council for the Promotion of International Trade, would lead a 16-strong team of executives and officials to Taiwan between October 14 and 20, the Commercial Times newspaper said.
The officials from China's Ministry of Foreign Trade and Economic Cooperation would visit as private citizens, although their itinerary included meetings with senior Taiwan officials.

On their list was a range of Taiwan government counterparts as well as the Nationalist-ruled island's top negotiator with Beijing, Koo Chen-fu, chairman of the quasi-official Straits Exchange Foundation, the reports said.
The economics ministry announced in September it was easing rules to allow more visits from China's business circles.
Taiwan has banned all direct official contact with communist China since the end of the Chinese civil war in 1949 when the Nationalist Republic of China was driven into exile on Taiwan.
Despite the ban, indirect commerce has flourished since the late 1980s when political tensions started to thaw. Some 30,000 Taiwan firms have poured more than US$20 billion into China.
High-level but "unofficial" Taiwan-China contacts have continued despite a freeze on more formal contacts that was ordered by Beijing in mid-1995.

Jing Shuping, head of Beijing's state-sanctioned All-China Federation of Industry and Commerce, reportedly plans to attend a meeting of entrepreneurs from China, Taiwan and Hong Kong to be held in Taipei in December.
In August, Taiwan tycoon Kao Ching-yung led nearly 80 Taiwan business leaders and politicians to Beijing to meet President and Communist Party chief Jiang Zemin and other leaders.
Taiwan's President Lee Teng-hui has urged caution, saying the island needed to review its policy of targeting China as its main market to avoid over-dependence on mainland investment.
